segments.t: DE
Terminal sessionsKTPH000

KorTTY provides a tabbed terminal interface with support for multiple simultaneous SSH connections, split-screen layouts, and interactive terminal management features. This guide covers tab operations, multi-window support, terminal customization, and advanced session features.
Session lifecycleKTPH000
The following diagram shows the terminal tab and session lifecycle, including split-screen and broadcast modes.
KTPH000
Working with tabsKTPH000
Manage multiple SSH sessions with these tab operations:
Action
Shortcut
KTPH000New TabKTPH001
KTPH002KTPH000KTPH003+KTPH004KTPH001KTPH005 (Cmd+T on macOS) — opens Quick Connect to start a new session
KTPH000Rename TabKTPH001

Right-click a tab and choose KTPH003Rename Tab…KTPH004, or use KTPH005File → Rename Tab…KTPH006 for the active tab. The name you enter replaces the connection's name, or the KTPH007title the shell setKTPH008, in the tab title; the coding-agent glyph, the KTPH000 prefix and the KTPH001 suffix stay around it. Leave the name empty, or confirm the name the tab shows on its own, and the tab follows the shell's title and the connection's name again, including later changes to them. While the shell names the tab, entering the connection's name keeps that name in place. A name can be up to 120 characters long; line breaks become spaces, and control characters and the invisible bidi controls that make text read in a different order are removed. The name is saved with a KTPH009projectKTPH010, and the KTPH011Coding AgentsKTPH012 panel and the Control API's KTPH013KTPH002KTPH014 show it; KTPH015DuplicateKTPH016 opens the copy under the connection's name. There is no shortcut, so every key stays with the program in the terminal.
KTPH000Title from the shellKTPH001

A terminal tab shows the title its shell sets, such as KTPH000, in place of the connection's name, unless you renamed the tab; pointing at it shows the connection it belongs to. See KTPH001Title from the shellKTPH002 below; it can be switched off in the KTPH003Window settingsKTPH004.
KTPH000Close TabKTPH001

KTPH002KTPH000KTPH003+KTPH004KTPH001KTPH005 (Cmd+W on macOS) — closes the active tab. You are only asked to confirm when there is something to lose: the tab has split panes, or a command is still running (a local shell with a running child process, or an SSH session that is not at its prompt). An idle single terminal closes immediately. The tab's close button and KTPH006CloseKTPH007 in the Dashboard ask the same question. The per-connection KTPH008Close tab without confirmationKTPH009 setting suppresses the prompt entirely.
KTPH000Close Other Tabs / Close Tabs to the RightKTPH001

Right-click a terminal tab and choose KTPH000Close Other TabsKTPH001 or KTPH002Close Tabs to the RightKTPH003, or use the KTPH004FileKTPH005 menu entries of the same name, which act around the active tab of any kind. KTPH006Close Other TabsKTPH007 closes every other tab of the window, KTPH008Close Tabs to the RightKTPH009 the tabs after it; the tab you chose stays open and becomes the active tab. An entry is greyed out while there is nothing to close. Instead of one question per tab you are asked at most once, KTPH010Close N tabs?KTPH011, with the number of them that have split panes or a command that is still running. Closing only idle terminals and other tabs asks nothing, just like their close buttons, and the KTPH012Close active terminal windows without confirmationKTPH013 setting on the KTPH014Terminal settingsKTPH015 tab silences the question as it does for KTPH016Close All TabsKTPH017. A file or snippet editor with unsaved changes still asks on its own (Save / Discard / Cancel), and a Cancel at any question keeps every tab open. A running AI chat request or swarm in a closing tab stops, as with its close button. There is no shortcut.
KTPH000Reopen Closed TabKTPH001

KTPH007KTPH001KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH002KTPH010+KTPH011KTPH003KTPH012+KTPH013KTPH004KTPH014 (Cmd+Option+Shift+T on macOS), KTPH015File → Reopen Closed TabKTPH016 or KTPH017Reopen Closed TabKTPH018 in a terminal tab's right-click menu brings back the terminal tab you closed last, with a new session to the same connection: its tab group, the name you gave it and its terminal effect come back, its output and its split panes do not. KTPH019File → Recently ClosedKTPH020 lists what you closed in this session, newest first; choose an entry to reopen it, or KTPH021Clear ListKTPH022 to empty the list. Each close is one entry: a single tab (its close button, KTPH023Close TabKTPH024 or KTPH025CloseKTPH026 in the Dashboard); all the terminal tabs that one KTPH027Close Other TabsKTPH028, KTPH029Close Tabs to the RightKTPH030 or KTPH031Close All TabsKTPH032 closed, which reopen together; or the terminal tabs of a window you closed while korTTY kept running, shown as KTPH033Window: …KTPH034, which reopen in a new window, or in the current one when it has no tabs. On macOS, where korTTY keeps running after you close its last window, KTPH035File → Reopen Closed TabKTPH036 and KTPH037File → Recently ClosedKTPH038 in the menu bar open a new window for what they reopen. Tabs whose session ended on their own (KTPH000, KTPH039KTPH005KTPH040+KTPH041KTPH006KTPH042), the tabs that opening a KTPH043projectKTPH044 replaces and everything that closes when you quit korTTY are not listed. The list holds the last 25 closes for all windows together and is kept in memory only, so it is gone when korTTY quits. A reopened tab signs in like KTPH045ConnectKTPH046 in the Connection Manager (see KTPH047Signing inKTPH048) and uses the saved connection with the changes you made since, so the KTPH049server access policyKTPH050 is checked again; a login method you chose for that one session in Quick Connect is not repeated. A Quick Connect session that was never saved reopens with the settings it had. The list never keeps a temporary SSH key, so a session that used one asks for a new key. If you cancel a password, key or vault question, the entry stays in the list. The key works in every tab, also while a terminal has the focus and with the menu bar hidden; when there is nothing to reopen, the status bar says so.
KTPH000Bell markKTPH001

When a program rings the terminal bell or asks for a notification in a tab you are not looking at, the tab shows 🔔 in its title until you select it or bring its window to the front, and a desktop notification can show as well. See KTPH000Terminal notificationsKTPH001.
KTPH000Next TabKTPH001

++ctrl+Tab++ (KTPH004KTPH000KTPH005 on macOS too). With KTPH006Ctrl+Tab switches tabs in the order they were last usedKTPH007 on in the KTPH008Window settingsKTPH009, it goes back to the tab you used before the current one instead; keep KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011 held and press KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013 again to go further back, and release KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015 at the tab you want.
KTPH000Previous TabKTPH001
++ctrl+shift+Tab++, or with the same setting on, the tab you used longest ago, stepping towards the recent ones while KTPH001KTPH000KTPH002 stays held
KTPH000Jump to a tabKTPH001

KTPH012KTPH000KTPH013+KTPH014KTPH001KTPH015 to KTPH016KTPH002KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH003KTPH019 (KTPH020KTPH004KTPH021 on macOS) select the first to eighth tab of the window and KTPH022KTPH005KTPH023+KTPH024KTPH006KTPH025 the last one, with the digits of the top row or the numpad. The keys work in every tab, also while the terminal has the focus, and a number with no tab at its position does nothing. No digit is typed into the terminal, nor in KTPH026broadcast modeKTPH027 into the other panes. On Windows and Linux only KTPH028KTPH007KTPH029 with a digit jumps, so KTPH030KTPH008KTPH031 characters and KTPH032KTPH009KTPH033+KTPH034KTPH010KTPH035+KTPH036KTPH011KTPH037 still reach the terminal; see KTPH038Keyboard shortcutsKTPH039 for the layout details.
KTPH000ReconnectKTPH001

Right-click a tab, the terminal area, or a server entry in the Dashboard. If the connection is active, it is closed and re-established immediately; if disconnected, it is re-established. The terminal window stays open.
KTPH000Tab GroupsKTPH001

Right-click a tab to assign it to a named group for better organization; KTPH000No GroupKTPH001 takes it out of its group again. The same menu offers KTPH002DuplicateKTPH003, which opens another tab to the same connection and signs in like the Connection Manager (see KTPH004Signing inKTPH005).
KTPH000Tab colorKTPH001

A connection with a KTPH000tab colorKTPH001 marks each of its terminal tabs with a colored dot in front of the title and a 3-pixel frame of that color around the terminal, for example red for production servers. The frame surrounds all split panes of the tab and can be switched off in the KTPH002Window settingsKTPH003; turning it on or off resizes the terminal by 3 pixels on each side. Pointing at such a tab shows a tooltip with the connection and the color by name, which screen readers read for the dot as well. Set the color in the connection editor on the KTPH004Terminal SettingsKTPH005 tab; saving it in the Connection Manager updates the open tabs in every window. A connection without a color of its own can show the color of its stored credential's KTPH006environmentKTPH007 instead. The yellow tab of a connection being made and the dark red tab of a failed or lost connection are unchanged.
Title from the shellKTPH000

Many shells and programs set a terminal title with the OSC 0 or OSC 2 escape sequence: the default KTPH000 of Debian and Ubuntu puts KTPH001 there, and editors or coding agents put the file or the task. A terminal tab shows that title in place of the connection's name, with the coding-agent glyph, the KTPH002 prefix and the KTPH003 suffix around it as usual. A tab with split panes shows the title of the pane that has the focus, and switches when you move to another pane.
A name you gave the tab with KTPH000Rename TabKTPH001 always comes first. Clear that name again and the tab follows the shell's title once more.
Pointing at a tab named by its shell shows a tooltip with the connection it belongs to: KTPH000 and the connection's name.

Connecting safelyKTPH000

Interactive SSH terminals share host-key trust with SFTP and the SSH bootstrap used by Mosh. The first connection to a normalized host and port shows the key algorithm and OpenSSH SHA-256 fingerprint with KTPH000NoKTPH001 selected by default. After you verify and accept it, exact matches connect silently; a changed key is hard-blocked with no automatic retry, and the alert offers KTPH002Review and Replace…KTPH003 for a key you have verified with the server administrator. See KTPH004SSH host-key verificationKTPH005.

Opening a same-server or newly selected connection in a split shows a progress dialog while the SSH handshake runs on a worker. The interface remains responsive for both the host-key confirmation and keyboard-interactive authentication prompts.

KTPH000Split Right (new connection)KTPH001 and KTPH002Split Down (new connection)KTPH003 follow your organization's KTPH004server access policyKTPH005 like Quick Connect: if the server you pick or its jump server is blocked, korTTY shows the policy message right away, before it asks for a password or saves the connection, and opens no pane. KTPH006Split Right (same server)KTPH007 and KTPH008Split Down (same server)KTPH009 check the policy again for the server of the pane you split: a pane opened from a saved connection can pick up later edits of it, so if its server or jump server was edited to a blocked one after the pane opened, the split shows the same message and opens no pane.

Some failures are refused outright rather than retried, because repeating the attempt cannot change the outcome — a changed host key, an SSH key file that is missing or cannot be read, a jump server whose stored password cannot be used (for example while the vault is locked) or whose setup is incomplete, a Mosh connection configured with a jump server, or a missing Mosh runtime. The terminal clears and shows the reason immediately instead of working through the retry count. See KTPH000Jump serverKTPH001 for the jump-server cases and the Mosh restriction.

KorTTY's pinned SithTermFX build also includes a reviewed bottom-row boundary fix: moving over a hyperlink or the final visible terminal row no longer asks KTPH000 for the non-existent row at KTPH001.
Connection loss and automatic reconnectKTPH000

When an KTPH004establishedKTPH005 SSH connection is lost — network drop, VPN cut, server gone — the tab does KTPH006notKTPH007 close. It switches to a red disconnected state instead: the tab title gets a KTPH000 suffix, the tab turns dark red, a red status bar shows the time the connection was lost, and the terminal cursor stops blinking so a dead session no longer looks alive. Only a normal remote logout (typing KTPH001, or KTPH008KTPH002KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH003KTPH011 at the prompt) closes the tab.

KorTTY notices a silent transport death within about ten seconds: every few seconds it sends an SSH liveness probe (a global request the server must answer, the same technique as OpenSSH's KTPH000) and treats two consecutive unanswered probes as a lost connection. The probe only arms itself after the server has answered once, so servers that never reply to such requests keep their sessions untouched. This is independent of the KTPH001SSH keep-aliveKTPH002 heartbeat, which keeps idle connections open but does not detect a dead one.

To pick the session back up in the same tab, double-click the red status bar or the red tab, or use KTPH000ReconnectKTPH001 in the tab, terminal, or Dashboard context menu or in the KTPH002command paletteKTPH003. In a split tab, panes whose connection died close individually; the last remaining pane keeps the tab open and carries the reconnect offer.

With KTPH000Automatically reconnect lost connectionsKTPH001 enabled (KTPH002Settings → TerminalKTPH003, on by default), the tab reconnects on its own: attempts start after 3 seconds and back off through 5, 10, 20 and 30 seconds up to one attempt per minute, and the red status bar counts down to the next attempt. A successful reconnect, a manual reconnect, or closing the tab ends the automatic attempts. Permanent failures — authentication, host-key verification, configuration refusals — stop them too, so a wrong password is never hammered against the server. While a KTPH004session journalKTPH005 is running, its red decision bar takes precedence and no automatic attempt starts — the journal asks whether to reconnect and continue or to end with its closing summary. See KTPH006Settings → TerminalKTPH007 for the setting.

Pasting textKTPH000

Every way of pasting into a terminal goes through korTTY: KTPH005Edit → PasteKTPH006, KTPH007KTPH000KTPH008+KTPH009KTPH001KTPH010 on macOS, KTPH011KTPH002KTPH012+KTPH013KTPH003KTPH014+KTPH015KTPH004KTPH016 on Windows and Linux, KTPH017PasteKTPH018 in the right-click menu, a middle-click, which pastes the X11 primary selection on Linux and the clipboard elsewhere, and text you KTPH019drop onto a paneKTPH020. The text goes to the pane you paste into, and its line breaks arrive as Enter, the way they do when you type them.

When the program in the pane has switched on bracketed paste, as bash, zsh, fish and most editors do while they wait for input, korTTY wraps the text in the bracketed-paste markers. The program then receives it as one pasted block instead of typed keys, so a line break in it does not run a command on its own. Bracketed-paste markers inside the text itself are removed first, including the 8-bit form that a single-byte KTPH000character encodingKTPH001 sends, so text copied from a web page or a file can neither end the paste early nor have its remaining lines run as typed commands.

After a reconnect, and after a terminal reset (the KTPH000 command, or KTPH001 in the output), a pane does not use bracketed paste until its program switches it on again, so pasted line breaks act as Enter until then. A Mosh connection that recovers from a network interruption continues the same session and keeps the state.

Some pastes ask before they reach the pane. korTTY then shows what you are about to paste, and nothing is sent until you choose KTPH000PasteKTPH001. Which pastes ask is set under KTPH002Settings → Terminal → Paste protectionKTPH003 (see KTPH004Terminal settingsKTPH005):

KTPH000Line breaksKTPH001: by default a paste with a line break asks unless the program in the pane uses bracketed paste, because each line break would then act as Enter and run a command. A single line that ends in a line break asks as well, since it would run at once. With KTPH002AlwaysKTPH003, every paste with a line break asks, bracketed or not; with KTPH004OffKTPH005, none does.

The terminal on the server acts on Ctrl+C, Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+S before the program sees the paste, and direction-changing characters make text look different from what is sent. Switches, routers, console servers and other devices behind SSH can lose input that arrives faster than they read it, so a pasted configuration arrives with characters or whole lines missing. A single line still goes out at once, and a paste that asks for confirmation is paced after you choose KTPH004PasteKTPH005.

While the lines are sent, the bottom right corner of the pane shows how far the paste is, such as KTPH002Pasting line 3 of 40 · Esc stopsKTPH003. The pane takes no keyboard input meanwhile, so nothing you type lands between two pasted lines; on macOS, KTPH004KTPH000KTPH005 shortcuts keep working, and the pane's find bar still takes what you type. Press KTPH006KTPH001KTPH007 to stop the paste: the remaining lines are not sent. When the program in the pane uses bracketed paste, the paced lines still arrive as one pasted block, and stopping ends that block, so the lines already sent stay in the program's input line without running.

Drag text from another application, such as a browser or an editor, or from another korTTY window, and drop it onto a terminal pane to paste it there. It goes into the pane under the pointer, which need not be the pane you were typing in, and that pane becomes the focused pane. KTPH000Quick Connect KTPH002 Terminal logKTPH001 for a one-off session, or to change the setting for the connection you are about to open.

Quick Connect's Terminal log section covers enable, folder, format and compression; size limit, retention and daily rotation keep their configured or default values.
File namesKTPH000

Every file is named KTPH000, for example KTPH001. The date leads so a folder listing sorts chronologically, and the trailing number distinguishes connections that are open at the same time — two tabs on the same server get KTPH002 and KTPH003 and never write into one another's file.
Rotation, compression and retentionKTPH000

By default a new file is started KTPH002every dayKTPH003, and always again whenever the maximum size is reached (those parts are numbered KTPH000, KTPH001, …); daily rotation can be turned off to roll only by size. Nothing is ever overwritten or deleted by rotation.

Closed files are gzipped by default; the file currently being written always stays uncompressed so that a crash cannot truncate it. Turn off KTPH000Compress closed files (gzip)KTPH001 to keep finished files as plain text instead. A connection that produces no output creates no file at all.

Files older than the retention period are deleted automatically when a connection starts and after each daily rollover. Set the retention to KTPH000 to keep everything. Only KorTTY's own log files are ever removed — anything else in the folder is left alone, so it is safe to point the setting at a folder you also use for other things.
What is removed before writingKTPH000

Captured lines go through the same redaction as the KTPH000Session JournalKTPH001, on the capture thread, before anything is buffered or written: the connection's own password and any replacement rules your organisation's policy defines. The secret never reaches the file, so there is nothing to clean up afterwards.
Log files and a log folder KorTTY created itself are set to owner-only permissions where the filesystem supports it. A folder you chose yourself is left with the permissions you gave it.
Redaction only covers what KorTTY knows

A password KorTTY stores for the connection is redacted. A secret you type into a command yourself, or one a program prints, is not — KorTTY has no way to recognise it. Treat the log folder as sensitive, and use policy replacement rules for patterns that recur.
